title: Your faith has made you well (Luke 8:40–56)
hook: a bleeding woman and a dying girl, twelve years each

segments.voice: Yesterday, a storm on the lake and a man among the tombs, sent home. Your line was return to your house. Whose storm did you help calm? Day five hundred thirty-three.

Twelve years. That's the number tying today's two stories together. A man named Jairus, a ruler of the local synagogue, an important man in town, falls at Jesus' feet. His only daughter, about twelve years old, is dying. Please come. Jesus goes, and the crowd presses so tightly around him that it's hard to move. And somewhere in that crush is a woman nobody notices, who has been bleeding for twelve years. As long as Jairus's daughter has been alive, this woman has been sick. Luke says she had spent everything she had on doctors, and none of them could heal her. She doesn't ask for anything. She has a plan.

Under the law of her time, her bleeding made her ritually unclean, and for twelve years that would have kept her at the edges of worship and of ordinary touch. So she comes up from behind and, in the King James words, "touched the border of his garment: and immediately her issue of blood stanched." She just wanted to slip away. But Jesus stops. "Who touched me?" Peter points out the obvious: Master, the whole crowd is pressing against you! But Jesus says, "Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me." Virtue here means power. Trembling, she comes forward and tells everything in front of everyone. And Jesus says: "Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace." Daughter. A family word for a woman who had been kept at the edges, said in public, so the whole town hears that she is well. Made thee whole is the Greek sozo. It's the same phrase as "thy faith hath saved thee," said to the woman at Simon's dinner. Healed and saved share one word. But the stop has cost time. A messenger arrives: "Thy daughter is dead; trouble not the Master." Jesus hears it and says: "Fear not: believe only, and she shall be made whole." At the house, the mourners are already wailing. He says she's sleeping, and they laugh at him. He takes her hand: "Maid, arise." She gets up. And then a very practical line: he tells them to give her something to eat.
screen: `SHE TOUCHED THE BORDER OF HIS GARMENT.`
`DAUGHTER: THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.`
then, large: `FEAR NOT: BELIEVE ONLY, AND SHE SHALL BE MADE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold two people at once. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind two people who need help right now. One might be loud about it, like Jairus, important and urgent and asking. The other might be quiet, like the woman in the crowd, hidden, hoping nobody notices. Hold them both. Notice which one your attention runs to first. Then bring the other one forward, too. In the story, Jesus has time for both: he stops for the woman and still reaches the girl. Breathe in for one person, breathe out for the other, back and forth. If you pray, you can hold both before God together. If you don't, simply keep both in your care. The bell holds the time.
Sozo, the Greek word used for both healing and being saved: Jesus' words to a woman healed after twelve years, said on the way to a twelve-year-old girl he raises with a word, maid, arise.
Your line: only believe. Today, hold your two people together, and do one small thing for the quiet one. Day five hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray with the healing of the woman and Jairus's daughter when they or someone they love is ill, and in some churches prayer for the sick includes a gentle touch on the shoulder or hand.

fork.setup: you're hurrying to a dying girl. someone in the crowd touches your cloak and is healed. what do you do?
options: keep going; the girl can't wait.
stop and ask who touched you, and speak to her.
fork.reveal: Jesus stops, finds her, and calls her daughter in front of everyone. then he still reaches Jairus's house.

original.note: Greek: has saved, has made well. from sozo, used for healing and for salvation.

trapdoor: what you thought: a healing story with a happy ending.
what it means: Jesus stops for the hidden woman and makes her healing public, then raises a girl everyone else had given up on.
what a scholar hears: "thy faith hath made thee whole" here and "thy faith hath saved thee" at Simon's dinner (7:50) are the same Greek words, built on sozo.

notes: 'Daughter' (8:48) is described as a family word; the script avoids claiming it is unique (Mark 5:34 and Matthew 9:22 have it too).
Ritual impurity from Leviticus 15:25–27 described carefully ('at the edges of worship and of ordinary touch'). Keeper to confirm framing.
Some manuscripts of Luke 8:43 lack 'had spent all her living upon physicians'. The KJV includes it.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'Peter almost laughs' (not in 8:45), 'Imagine Jairus's face', and 'the most practical line in the Gospel'; the sozo point now rests on the identical Greek of 7:50 and 8:48 instead of a general claim; the practice no longer opens by telling the listener to pray.
